name: two keys, one slot
hook: What happens when two keys hash to the exact same slot?
hook_sub: Nobody gets turned away. The slot grows a chain.
caption: With {m} buckets, {a} and {b} both land in slot {slot_ab}. Collisions aren't a bug in your hash table. They're guaranteed.
Separate chaining: each bucket holds a list. Insert appends to that list; lookup scans only that one list.

That's why "O(1)" is an average. Put {prank_n} keys that all hash to slot {prank_slot} into one table and finding the last one scans {prank_scan} entries. Spread the same number of keys out and it's {spread_scan}.
Doubling the table helps, statistically: {c} and {d} split apart at {m2} buckets, but {a} and {b} still share slot {slot_ab2}.
Did you know the O(1) was an average? 👇
cta: Watch a chain form, then a rehash re-file every key.

p: A table with {m} buckets files a key under `key % {m}`. Two different keys, one address.
Sooner or later it is guaranteed to happen.
Insert appends to that bucket's list. Lookup scans only that one list, never the whole table.
The cost of any operation is the length of one chain.
Under uniform hashing, the expected chain length is the *load factor*: entries per bucket. Keep it bounded by resizing and the expected work stays constant.

rows.lab: Entries scanned to find the last one
Same number of keys, spread out

p: "Hash lookup is O(1)" quotes the average case, not a guarantee.
Doubling reduces collisions statistically, not individually.
